Brushing your teeth more than twice a day is not automatically harmful, but it can become problematic depending on frequency and technique [d1][d6]. According to Cleveland Clinic, "you can brush more than twice a day if you choose — but do it gently," and brushing after sugary or sticky foods is advisable [d1]. However, experts cited by BBC Future warn that "it might actually be harmful to brush more often than twice a day," as excessive brushing risks abrasion to the tooth [d6]. Multiple sources agree that brushing more than three times a day can wear down tooth enamel and damage gums, leading to sensitivity and increased cavity risk [d3][d4]. The specific risks of overbrushing include dental abrasion, tooth sensitivity, and gum recession, caused by both brushing too often and brushing too vigorously [d2][d5]. Exceptions exist for people wearing braces, clear aligners, or partial dentures, who may be advised to brush after each meal [d1][d6]. The general consensus from the ADA and leading dental organizations remains to brush twice a day, a frequency that prevents plaque buildup while also avoiding the problems associated with overbrushing [d7].
